title: Step toward accountability: Top UN court finds Myanmar guilty of Rohingya genocide
text:
Step toward accountability: Top UN court finds Myanmar guilty of Rohingya genocide
Rohingya refugees around the world welcomed the ruling, which comes after a yearslong legal battle and decades of persecution in western Myanmar.
For the first time in its history, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide.
Judge Yuji Iwasawa, president of the world’s highest court, said Thursday that its judges found “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.” The decision, reached in a 9-6 vote, ends a yearslong international legal battle for the majority-Muslim ethnic group.
The court ordered Myanmar to compensate the Rohingya, who have faced decades of discrimination and repression in western Myanmar, including restrictions on citizenship, movement, and access to basic services. The military has also been accused of widespread violence against the community – persecution that escalated during military operations in 2016 and 2017, when villages were burned, civilians killed, and women subjected to sexual violence. Today, about 1.2 million Rohingya live in cramped refugee camps in Bangladesh.
Proving genocide, as defined by the United Nations after the Nazi Holocaust, requires evidence of specific intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. Reading the judgment, Judge Iwasawa said the court was “fully convinced” that Myanmar’s government violated the 1948 Genocide Convention “with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar.”
At a time when trust in international law is wavering, the United Nations’ top court has delivered an unprecedented decision, finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against its Rohingya minority. It could impact similar cases around the world.
Rohingya refugees around the world welcomed the ruling.
“This is a historic moment for our Rohingya community,” says Kyaw Min Sabber, director of the advocacy group Rohingya Human Rights Initiative. “We have waited many years for this day, seeking justice, accountability, and recognition of the genocide committed against our people.”
The case was brought by Gambia in 2019, marking the first time a country with no direct connection to alleged atrocities filed a genocide case with the court. The resulting judgment establishes an authoritative legal finding of genocide, and formally recognizes the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group in Myanmar. (The government has previously described them as Bengali migrants.)
The court ordered Myanmar to take steps to prevent further violations of the Genocide Convention, investigate and prosecute those responsible, and provide reparations to the Rohingya, including allowing refugees to return home safely and voluntarily. However, the ruling does not automatically bring military leaders to trial or ensure displaced Rohingya can return. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism, and Myanmar’s compliance will depend partly on international pressure and action by the U.N. Security Council.
Still, the judgment carries considerable diplomatic and symbolic weight. It gives survivors legal recognition of the atrocities they endured, strengthens demands for accountability, and establishes a precedent for how the international community can respond to allegations of genocide moving forward – including how judges assess evidence in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel.
And it is a rare win for a community that has spent decades fighting to be heard.
“Today’s ICJ ruling represents an important step towards establishing accountability and ensuring that those responsible cannot escape justice,” says Kyaw Min Sabber, who fled persecution and now lives in Canada.
